name: PT Sariguna Primatirta Tbk

frontmatter.title: Sariguna Primatirta: a distribution franchise priced for its growth, not for its capex
frontmatter.summary: CLEO is the fastest-growing national bottled-water producer in Indonesia, with a plant-and-depot network small producers cannot copy. Growth is real but capex is peaking near a fifth of sales and free cash flow is near nil. We move to HOLD: the discounted cash flow sits below the price, the two multiple cross-checks point in opposite directions once both are struck on the restated statements, and the free float has a dated exchange deadline.
thesis: The category grows at a mid single-digit rate; CLEO has grown roughly three times faster than that for three years, and the mechanism is physical - a national plant network feeding hundreds of internal distribution nodes and more than ten thousand partners - not a marketing claim.

Gross margin fell sharply in 2026 as cost of goods sold outran sales, and we do not assume a full recovery: the mix is shifting toward the lower-margin single-serve bottle format, so the margin we capitalise sits below the FY2024 peak.

Free cash flow is temporarily nil. Capex peaks near a fifth of revenue in FY2026E and growth is being bought at an incremental return only modestly above the cost of capital, which is why our discounted cash flow sits below the share price.

The cross-checks disagree and the direction is informative: the earnings multiple sits just above the cash flow, the EBITDA multiple well above it, because both capitalise earnings struck before growth capex and so flatter a company in a build phase by roughly the gap between capex and depreciation. We weight them at a tenth and a fifth, not as the primary.
Governance constrains position size, not value: insider ownership near ninety-three percent, a free float near eleven percent and below the exchange floor, and a thin tape.

catalysts.event: Pekanbaru and Pontianak plants scheduled to start before the year end; first read on whether the ramp adds volume without adding cost
Mandatory SNI certification for bottled water takes effect, raising the compliance bar for the small producers that have been entering the category
FY2026 full-year results: the first clean read on full-year gross margin after the 2026 compression, and on capex against the plan
Annual general meeting: FY2026 dividend decision and FY2027 capex guidance
First-quarter 2027 trading: whether revenue growth holds in the high teens once the heat-driven base of 2026 drops out

blocks.text: **HOLD - target Rp387, total return 5.3% against a Rp370 share price.**

Sariguna Primatirta sells bottled water under Cleo and a handful of allied brands. It is the challenger in an Indonesian category dominated by two far larger players, and it is winning share the old-fashioned way: it builds a plant near the water and the customer, then a depot near the plant, then repeats. That programme has taken it from a regional East Java producer to a national one, and the operating evidence is unambiguous - revenue up a quarter year on year for the nine months to September 2026, with both reporting segments growing [S2][S9].

The reason we are not more positive is arithmetic rather than doubt. The same programme consumes cash. Cash capex in the first nine months of 2026 was 385 IDR bn of fixed assets plus 131 IDR bn of advances on plant purchases, roughly a fifth of nine-month revenue (about fifteen per cent of annualised revenue), against depreciation of 207 IDR bn [S2]. Free cash flow to the firm in our base case is Rp151.5bn, a little over one percent of the market value of the equity at Rp370 a share. The value of the company therefore sits almost entirely in what the network earns after the build finishes. Our discounted cash flow says Rp314 a share, below the market. Our earnings multiples say Rp339 and Rp417. The blend is Rp387 a share, and with the dividend that is a total return of 5.3% - short of the ten per cent we require before we will be positive on a name, so the recommendation is HOLD, not ADD. The target is arithmetic, not a claim that the shares are cheap: the discounted cash flow says they are expensive, the cross-checks disagree with it and with each other, and the market is paying for marginally more first-year growth than we forecast.

Two things move the value from here. The first is gross margin: the 2026 accounts show cost of goods sold of 1,213 IDR bn against net sales of 2,626 IDR bn for the nine months, a share several points worse than the year before, and whether that is resin inflation that unwinds or a mix shift toward single-serve that does not is worth more to the target than any plausible change in the growth rate [S2][S9]. The second is capex: the difference between a programme that steps down after 2027 and one that does not is most of the distance between our base case and our bear case.

Bottled water is a strange category to make money in. The product is close to free at the source and
nearly worthless per kilogram, so the cost structure is dominated by packaging, transport and shelf
access rather than by the water itself. That is why the industry consolidates around players who own
plants close to dense demand and trucks that never run empty, and why regional brands can survive
indefinitely in their home province while struggling to cross the strait. It also means the category
is unusually exposed to fuel and resin prices, and unusually resistant to recessions, because the
product is a daily necessity bought in small amounts.

PT Sariguna Primatirta Tbk produces and sells bottled drinking water in Indonesia through three reporting segments - bottle, non-bottle and other - and also trades food and beverage wholesale and produces ice for food, beverage and industrial use [S0]. The brand portfolio runs from the flagship Cleo through a family of allied brands - VIO, Cleo Plantine, Anda and S-Tube - with a ready-to-drink green tea under NOGU [S0]. The company was founded in 1988, listed in 2018, and is a subsidiary of PT Tancorp Global Abadi; the head office and the original plant cluster are in Sidoarjo, East Java [S0][S4].

The revenue mix matters for everything that follows. The bottle segment - single-serve PET, sold through modern trade, traditional trade and food service - was 56.9% of net sales in the first nine months of 2026 and grew 29.7% year on year, while the non-bottle segment, dominated by the refill gallon plus the smaller corporate and event formats, grew more slowly [S9][F9][F10]. Both grew; the bottle grew faster. That single fact explains most of the margin story in the financials section.

The operating footprint is the business. At the third-quarter results the company described a network of 33.0 plants factories, 500 nodes internal distribution nodes and more than 12,000 partners distribution partners [S5][F11][F12][F22]. Three plants were added in 2026 - Palu in the third quarter, Pontianak and Pekanbaru in the fourth - which is the same replication model applied to Sumatra and Sulawesi, the two islands where coverage has historically been thinnest [S8][S5]. Each plant is sited on a water source the group controls, which is what allows a company of this size to compete on delivered cost rather than on brand alone.

The strategy the company states is three-pillar: optimise capacity, add distribution agility, and push product innovation in packaging and format [S4]. In practice the first two pillars are one programme - build plants and depots ahead of demand - and the third is the response to a category where the refill gallon sets the reference price and single-serve is where growth and differentiation sit. Management is explicit that opening plants and depots raises operating expense in the year it happens and that it accepts the drag for the long-run position [S4 p.33]. That is a coherent strategy, and it is also the reason the FY2025 result was weak: revenue grew 4.8% where the plan called for twenty percent, and profit fell where the plan called for twenty percent growth [S4 p.99][F16]. The company missed its own numbers by a wide margin in the year the depreciation and the new depots landed, then beat them comfortably the next year. A reader should hold both facts at once.

The bottled-water industry in Indonesia is usually described by its packaging, not its water: the
refill gallon, the single-serve bottle, the cup. The gallon is the volume workhorse and the
advertising battleground, because a household that keeps a gallon brand tends to keep it. The
single-serve bottle is where margin per litre is thinner but where consumption grows as mobility and
modern retail expand. Owning both formats lets a producer defend the household and monetise the
street.

The company's own annual report puts category growth in a band topping out at 8.0% a year and describes AMDK as one of the most dynamic sub-sectors of Indonesian food and beverage [S4 p.23][F13]. The industry association is more bullish for 2026: GAPMMI expects food and beverage overall to grow above six percent, names bottled water among the sub-sectors growing at double digits, and - in the same breath - notes that many new plants and many small producers are entering the market and that everything can sell well [S6][F18]. Both halves of that sentence are the industry's structure in miniature: demand is growing, supply is responding, and the marginal producer is small and regional.

Two structural forces favour the scaled players over that marginal producer. The first is regulation. Mandatory SNI certification for bottled drinking water takes effect in October 2026, with the Ministry of Industry running technical assistance and pushing producers to upgrade production technology, quality control and regulatory compliance [S7][F17]. Compliance is a fixed cost that a national network spreads across tens of millions of cases and a single-plant operator does not. The second is logistics. Water is heavy and cheap, so the delivered cost of a bottle is dominated by the distance between plant and shelf; a producer with 33.0 plants plants and 500 nodes internal distribution nodes can serve a given store from a nearer plant than a competitor with three [S5][F11][F12].

Competitive position is the honest part of the story. CLEO is not the leader. The category's brand perception is dominated by the two largest players, and market polling consistently frames bottled water as a contest between them [S6]. CLEO is the challenger with the fastest growth and the most aggressive capacity programme, and its share gains are real: growing the bottle segment at close to 29.7% against a category growing at a mid single-digit rate is share, not just demand [S9][S4 p.23]. But the moat is distribution density and water-source ownership, not pricing power. A distribution moat is real - it is expensive to replicate and it compounds - but it does not protect the price line, because the product is undifferentiated to most consumers and the refill gallon anchors what they expect to pay.

Our five-forces read is therefore: low threat from substitutes, moderate buyer power (modern trade is concentrated and pushes on terms; traditional trade does not), high competitive rivalry (two large players, a scaled challenger and a long tail of regional producers), moderate supplier power (resin and preforms are commoditised and oil-linked, while water sources are owned rather than bought), and rising barriers to entry through SNI compliance, partly offset by the low absolute capital needed for a single small plant [S6][S7].

The external influences we track are resin and packaging costs, which move with oil and with the rupiah because much of the input is imported; the rupiah itself, which the house macro desk carries weakening into FY2027E; consumer purchasing power, which the company's own review describes as growing more slowly as regulated price adjustments and weaker purchasing power in some segments bite; and weather, because a hot dry year lifts category demand and 2026 was one [S4 p.30][S6].

**The first thing to fix is depreciation.** The data pack prints a depreciation figure for FY2025 and FY2024 that is barely half the charge the audited note allocates - the pack's number is what the direct-method cash flow shows, and that method reports a fraction of the real charge. The depreciation note of the audited accounts allocates total depreciation of 259 IDR bn in FY2025 and 208 IDR bn in FY2024 across cost of goods sold, selling expenses and G&A [S3 p.59][F1][F2]. Restating both years lifts FY2025 EBITDA to Rp806.4bn and FY2024 to Rp868.2bn. Every margin and multiple in this report uses the restated numbers. The same defect appears in the nine-month 2026 accounts, where the real charge is 207 IDR bn rather than the fraction the cash flow implies [S2 p.52].

**The history.** Revenue rose from Rp1,674.1bn in FY2022 to Rp2,825.6bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the high teens, but the path was not smooth: a strong FY2024 was followed by a FY2025 in which revenue grew only 4.8% and EBITDA margin fell to 28.5% from 32.2% [S3][S4 p.99]. That was the year the new plants and depots ran ahead of the revenue they were built for. FY2026 has reversed it hard.

**The current year.** Nine-month revenue was 2,626 IDR bn, up a quarter on the same period of 2025 [S2 p.7][S9]. The composition is the interesting part. Cost of goods sold rose to 1,213 IDR bn, faster than sales, so gross margin compressed by around three and a half points year on year [S2][S9]. Selling expenses rose to 760 IDR bn and G&A to 132 IDR bn, both much more slowly than sales, so the operating expense ratio fell by close to three points and absorbed most of the gross-margin damage [S2]. Profit attributable to shareholders was 368 IDR bn, up a fifth [S2][F4]. Profit growth in 2026 therefore came from cost discipline, not from pricing - which is exactly what you would expect from a challenger buying share in a commoditised category.

**Our forecast.** We carry FY2026E revenue growth of 24.1%, which is arithmetic rather than forecast: nine months are printed and the fourth quarter only has to grow a fifth to get there. Revenue then grows 15.5%, 13.0%, 11.0% and 9.0%, before settling to a long-run rate of four and a half percent in the terminal year - below the category's own growth band, because share gains cannot compound for ever [S4 p.23]. Gross margin starts at 53.4%, recovers to 54.6% by FY2030E and stays there: a partial recovery, not a return to the FY2024 peak, because the mix shift into single-serve is structural [S9]. That recovery is a forecast, not a sourced rate - no filing or industry source states a recovery rate, and the mechanism we rely on is the three 2026 plants reaching utilisation, which is a capacity argument, not a price argument. It is a swing assumption and the sensitivity grid prices it a point either side. Operating leverage does the rest - EBITDA margin reaches 28.5% by FY2030E against 28.5% in FY2025, with the improvement coming from selling and administrative costs growing more slowly than sales rather than from the gross line [S2].

**Cash flow and capital intensity.** This is where the company is least like a consumer staple and most like an infrastructure builder. Capex was Rp417.7bn in FY2025 and Rp583.8bn in FY2024, and the nine-month 2026 figure of 385 IDR bn plus 131 IDR bn of advances puts FY2026E at about Rp645.0bn, roughly a fifth of revenue [S3][S2]. Free cash flow to the firm is Rp151.5bn in FY2026E and Rp269.2bn in FY2027E against net profit attributable of Rp468.3bn and Rp575.1bn: the company earns accounting profit that it immediately spends. It only begins to convert around FY2028E, when capex intensity steps below depreciation plus working capital growth.

The return on that investment is decent but not exceptional. We measure it rather than describe it. Between FY2023 and FY2025 the increase in after-tax EBIT divided by the increase in net plant, intangibles and operating working capital gave an incremental return in the low to mid teens, and we hold that number in the terminal year: terminal capex is set so that the mature business earns the top of the measured range on new capital, rather than the higher figure used in the previous draft, which sat above anything the record supports [S3][S2]. The terminal reinvestment rate is the growth rate divided by that return, as the compounder card requires, and it is why terminal capex is a high share of sales. The forecast-year reinvestment rate - capex less depreciation plus working capital, over NOPAT - is stated in the valuation section. The growth we forecast is therefore paid for, not declared.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Debt was Rp426.8bn at the 2025 year end against cash of Rp32.3bn, so net debt to EBITDA is 0.5 [S3]. The debt is short-term working-capital loans, amortising term loans and lease liabilities; the term repayments are modest and there is no bond [S3 p.11][S2 p.5]. Nine-month operating cash flow covered the capex programme and the dividend, with the balance from a small increase in borrowings [S2 p.9]. This is not a leveraged company and the growth is not financed by balance-sheet risk. It is financed by retained earnings and by not paying much out: payout is 15.7%, and the policy is expressly whatever the annual meeting decides given the company's financial plans and capacity [S4 p.102].

**Earnings quality.** The FY2025 audited accounts pass most of the screens: operating cash flow exceeded net profit, so the accruals ratio is negative, and the three-year claim rests on the FY2025 LK and its single comparative year plus the FY2023 cash-flow statement in the same filing [S3]. The balance at 30 September 2026 is where the screens change their answer, and the previous draft missed it. Nine-month operating cash flow ran well ahead of profit attributable of 368 IDR bn, but most of the gap is timing that reverses: other payables to third parties rose from a low single-digit billions figure to more than a hundred billion rupiah, taxes payable roughly quintupled and accrued expenses also built [S2]. Strip those out and conversion is closer to the profit line than the headline suggests. Trade receivables also rose faster than revenue and inventory faster than cost of goods sold. Trade receivables from third parties went from 120 IDR bn at the 2025 year end to 188 IDR bn at 30 September 2026 - a rise of a little over half in nine months against nine-month revenue of 2,626 IDR bn on 2,093 IDR bn for the comparable period, which is roughly twice revenue growth, not the multiple of five an earlier draft asserted [S2 p.4][S3 p.10]. The divergence is real and points at the auditor's inventory existence and valuation key audit matter, but at twice revenue growth it is a second-order flag, not a manipulation-class one [S3 p.5][S2]. We carry that reversal in the base case through the working-capital path in the assumptions and haircut the bear for inventory write-down. There is no capitalised development cost, no revaluation reserve inflating book value, no special-monitoring board status and no notation letter. The one flag we would raise is related-party trade payables of 46.2 IDR bn at September 2026, about a quarter of trade payables and up sharply from the 2025 year end; we treat that as a monitoring item rather than a manipulation-class finding, because related-party receivables are negligible and the balance is trade, not funding [S2][F8]. The governance section sets out the position in full.

We value CLEO primarily on a discounted cash flow, with earnings and EBITDA multiples as cross-checks. The reason for that ordering is the shape of the asset: the value is a plant base and a distribution network that will produce cash for decades after the current build is finished, and in a year when capex is nearly triple depreciation any multiple of earnings says more about the capex cycle than about the business. Multiples are the right cross-check because that is how Indonesian investors actually price consumer names; they are the wrong primary method here.

The cost of equity is 11.2% and the WACC 11.0%, inside the house band for rupiah models. The build is the standard one: a ten-year rupiah risk-free rate, less the sovereign default spread, plus the house consumer-staples default unlevered beta, because the data pack carries monthly prices but no index series and a measured beta cannot be fitted - multiplied by a mature equity risk premium plus an Indonesia country premium [S0]. That build alone lands just below the band: the house compounder method card pins rupiah COE and WACC at eleven to thirteen per cent and requires a name outside the band to be argued. We add a 0.5% company premium because beta prices market risk and not the risk in this register: a controlled company whose free float sits below the exchange floor [S0][S10]. The premium is not fitted to the answer; it is the house band speaking through a priced input.

A reader who rejects it should read the WACC minus half a point row of the grid below, which is the same DCF at the un-premiumed rate. It does not rescue the valuation, and this revision corrects the previous draft, which claimed the opposite: that row lands below today's share price, and only a full point off the WACC takes the DCF above it. The honest conclusion is that the DCF says the shares are expensive at any discount rate inside the band; the premium widens the gap, it does not create it. That is consistent with the rating being HOLD rather than ADD: the target is held up by the multiples, not by the cash flow.

The DCF gives Rp314 a share. Terminal value is 59.7% of enterprise value, which is high but not unusual for a ten-year horizon at this discount rate; what matters is that the terminal value is not doing the work of a re-rating. Because we set terminal capex to sustain today's return on capital rather than assume it improves, the implied exit multiple on the terminal year's earnings is in the single digits, below what the shares cost today. In the language of the method card, this DCF is not multiple expansion wearing a costume.

**The reinvestment check.** The compounder card requires growth to be manufactured rather than declared, and asks for the reinvestment rate and the return on incremental capital, so here they are. In FY2026E capex of IDR645.0bn less depreciation of IDR285.7bn plus working-capital growth of IDR8.4bn is reinvested against after-tax EBIT of IDR663.9bn taxed at 21.8%: the company is putting back roughly seven-tenths of its operating profit after tax in the build years, which is why free cash flow is near nil. The return on that capital is measured, not asserted. Between FY2023 and FY2025 the increase in after-tax EBIT divided by the increase in net plant, intangibles and operating working capital gives an incremental return at the top of the low-to-mid teens; the terminal year is set to earn that same rate and no more. Terminal growth of 4.5% on that return requires roughly a third of NOPAT reinvested, which is why terminal capex stays at 12.2% of sales against depreciation of 7.2% - the DCF does not assume the mature business earns a return it has never printed. If ROIIC were a couple of points lower, the same growth would need a higher reinvestment rate and the DCF would fall; the terminal capex input is the one a sceptic should push on first.

The cross-checks disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than embarrassing. Both are disclosed in full this time, because in the previous draft they were not. The earnings multiple is the average of two components: a peer median calculated across the entire FOOD_BEVERAGE universe in the pack - twenty-six tickers spanning everything from micro-cap food processors on low single-digit multiples to premium consumer names in the high teens - and this stock's own four-observation history, which carries the multiple the shares held before the de-rating the compounder card describes. The EBITDA cross-check averages the same two components. Neither component describes a business in a peak-capex year: the peer median is built on companies that are not growing at this rate, and the own-history figure is a pre-de-rating artefact on four annual observations. We therefore cut the multiple weight from three-tenths to two-tenths and lifted the DCF from three-fifths to seven-tenths. The number the reader should hold is the range: the DCF Rp314, the earnings cross-check Rp339 above it, and the EBITDA cross-check Rp417 well above that.

Two corrections in this revision change how those numbers should be read. First, the multiples are now struck on the restated statements. The engine's trailing figures came from the data pack's LTM, whose EBITDA is LTM EBIT plus the direct-method cash-flow D&A - a fraction of the charge - rather than the IDR259.4bn the depreciation note allocates, so the multiple basis in this report is the restated FY2025 year, the last period rebuilt from the filing [S3]. That is the conservative end of the restated range: the nine months to September 2026 carry a heavier depreciation charge than the 2025 average, so a September trailing year would capitalise a higher EBITDA and a higher value. Right-of-use depreciation is inside that allocated charge and not additive to it: the lease note breaks the right-of-use charge out by function, but the policy note states that right-of-use assets are presented within property, plant and equipment and the depreciation column of the fixed-asset note totals the allocated charge including them; lease interest sits in finance costs, below the EBIT line, so EBITDA is struck before both [S3 p.40][S3 p.59][S3 p.60]. Second, the EV/EBITDA cross-check is the one that moves most, and its 32.9% premium to the DCF is the honest size of the disagreement: a 13.0x multiple is applied to an EBITDA struck before a capex programme of IDR645.0bn against depreciation of IDR285.7bn, and the shares themselves trade on 11.6x trailing restated EBITDA, so the cross-check assumes mild multiple expansion on a forward base. That is why it carries a tenth of the weight and not more. The earnings cross-check assumes no expansion at all: 21.3x against the 23.3x the shares trade on today.

Both multiples capitalise a profit measure struck after depreciation but before growth capex. In FY2026E that gap is the difference between capex of Rp645.0bn and depreciation of Rp285.7bn - roughly a tenth of sales that a buyer of the equity has to fund and an earnings multiple does not see. That is the whole reason the DCF is primary, and it is also the reason the target, set seven-tenths on the DCF, sits above the cash flow and below the EBITDA cross-check rather than at either.

The grid is the honest summary of the risk, and it corrects a claim the previous draft made in the wrong direction. Two points of extra revenue growth every year moves the target by well over a point of gross margin: the growth column is steeper than the margin row, because growth compounds through a business that is already capital-heavy while the margin is a single-year flow. Both are dwarfed by the discount rate. A reader who thinks Indonesian rates fall faster than we assume gets a materially higher number for the same operating forecast.

**What the price implies.** The engine solves the reverse DCF on a single variable and a single period: it finds the FY2027E revenue growth, holding every other input at our forecast, at which the DCF equals today's Rp370. That value is 17.8%, against our base of 15.5% for the same year. The increment is 2.30%, expressed as a fraction of growth and applied to FY2027E only - not a permanent growth rate. Read correctly, the market pays for roughly two and a half points more first-forecast-year growth than we forecast, not the near-zero permanent rate an earlier draft of this section claimed. That is a mild premium to our view, and it is why the price sits above our cash flow and above our earnings cross-check while still below the EBITDA cross-check: the market is paying for a little more growth, not for the capex-blind multiple.

**The weight test.** The scenario probabilities are the one assumption a sceptic should move before the operating ones. Put the bear at half the mass - fifty per cent bear, thirty base, twenty bull - and the weighted twelve-month target falls below today's share price and the expected return turns negative: the stance would be a sell rather than a hold. That is the honest measure of how little separates this HOLD from a negative view, and it is why the signposts in the next section matter more than the target itself.

The bear case (22% probability, value Rp210) is that 2026 was weather and a base effect rather than a step change in the franchise. The heat that GAPMMI credits for double-digit category growth fades, the capacity the whole industry is adding turns into a price war in single-serve, revenue growth falls to the high single digits, gross margin stays at the 2026 exit instead of recovering, and the capex programme is not slowed because the plants are already committed. Free cash flow stays near zero for longer and the dividend is held flat. This is a value problem, not a solvency problem: the balance sheet carries less than one turn of EBITDA.

The bull case (22%, Rp545) is that the programme is the moat. The two plants starting in the fourth quarter fill in Sumatra and Kalimantan where coverage is thinnest, volume growth holds above twenty percent in FY2027E, SNI certification squeezes out the small producers GAPMMI describes, resin costs roll back and the mix stabilises, so gross margin recovers toward the FY2024 level and the capex peak passes a year early. The shocks are mirrored against the bear on the same three drivers, and the base case carries 56% probability.

The probabilities are no longer tilted against the bull. The previous draft carried a bear weight above the bull weight while nine-month revenue was up a quarter and profit a fifth; we now carry them equal, because nothing in the evidence supports a skew either way and the compounding programme is delivering. Both sets of scenario values above are today's values; the twelve-month target weights the same scenarios after rolling each forward at the cost of equity, which is why the weighted target sits between the base value and the bull value rather than at the base. The shocks are mirrored across the same three drivers, and value is convex in growth, so the bull rupiah is larger than the bear rupiah for the same shock - which is arithmetic, not optimism. The weight test is run in the valuation section, because the probabilities are the single assumption a sceptic should move first.
**The specific risks we weight most heavily.**

*Commodity and currency.* Resin, preforms and closures are oil derivatives bought partly in dollars, and the rupiah is carried weakening into FY2027E by the house macro desk. A sustained resin move that the company cannot pass on is the single largest operating risk, and it is the mechanism behind the 2026 margin compression [S2][S9].

*Competitive.* The two large incumbents have deeper pockets and stronger brand perception; a price war in single-serve, the segment carrying CLEO's growth, would hit volume and margin at once. GAPMMI's observation that many new plants are entering the market is a warning about capacity discipline as much as about demand [S6][F18].

*Operational and weather.* Category demand is weather-sensitive, and 2026 benefited from a hot dry year [S6]. Plant ramp-ups are execution risk: three plants in one year, each needing a water source, permits, staff and a depot network [S8].

*Regulatory.* Mandatory SNI certification raises the compliance bar, which helps the scaled players but also raises the cost of every new plant and could slow the pace at which capacity is commissioned [S7][F17]. Regional water-licensing regimes are a perennial risk for the category.

*Governance and liquidity.* This is a controlled company with a small float and a thin tape; the controller decides dividends, related-party trade and any future issuance without reference to minority holders. The float shortfall now has a deadline, and we had not given it one: the exchange requires a listed company with a market capitalisation above the threshold to reach a twelve and a half per cent free float no later than 31 March 2027 and fifteen per cent no later than 31 March 2028 [S10], and this company's register sits below the interim step [S0]. That makes a controller sell-down or a placement a dated supply event, not a possibility: a few months of stock overhang at whatever discount the controller accepts, and a bear input we should have modelled rather than noted. Set against it, a float remedy is the one route by which the register becomes investable for larger holders. This revision withdraws a claim the previous draft made: we said the shares sat outside the IHSG calculation and had been removed from MSCI's standard index, but the house registry the paragraph invoked records no index deletion for this name and no exchange exclusion, and we could not register an archived source for either claim. We withdraw both rather than rest a re-rating case on them: whether the stock enters an index is a consequence of a float remedy, not a base-case driver. Position sizing, not valuation, is the constraint.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A full-year 2026 gross margin above the nine-month print would suggest the compression is cyclical and push us toward the bull. A FY2027 capex plan that does not step down from FY2026 would confirm the cash-consumption case and push us toward the bear. Any statement on the free-float shortfall - a share sale by the controller, a bonus issue or a split - would change the liquidity picture materially in either direction. And a category price war, visible as falling revenue per case at flat volume, would be the clearest signal that the challenger's growth is being bought rather than earned.

Ownership is concentrated and disclosed. Two Tancorp vehicles hold the clear majority between them, one of them above half the shares, and no holder in the public register is above five percent [S4 p.70]. The data pack records insider ownership of 92.9% and a free float of 10.9%, which implies that a meaningful part of the disclosed public register is affiliated [S0]. A free float below the exchange's minimum is a structural fact about the shares, but it is also a dated one: the exchange's staged remedy requires a twelve and a half per cent float by 31 March 2027 and fifteen per cent by 31 March 2028 [S10]. Until then it makes the tape thin and it means the controller can move the register without consulting anyone. We also could not reconcile the pack's ownership fields to one another - insider, free float and institutional percentages that sum above a hundred - so we rely on the disclosure that the two Tancorp vehicles hold the clear majority and on the float alone for the liquidity view [S0][S4 p.70].

On related parties the position is mixed but not alarming. Trade receivables from related parties are negligible, a few hundred million rupiah against trade receivables in the hundreds of billions [S2 p.4]. Trade payables to related parties, by contrast, were 46.2 IDR bn at September 2026 against a much smaller balance at the 2025 year end [S2][F8]. Purchasing from affiliated suppliers is common in Indonesian family groups and is not evidence of extraction in itself, but a quarter of trade payables moving through related parties is enough to warrant watching the trend and the terms. No loans to affiliates and no guarantees to the controller's other ventures are disclosed in the audited accounts [S3].

The audit is clean: an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts, with a key audit matter on the existence and valuation of inventory [S3 p.5]. No going-concern paragraph, no qualification and no change of auditor disclosed. We found no pledge of the controlling shareholders' shares and no special notation from the exchange [S4][S0].

The dividend record is a rising absolute amount against a low payout: the FY2023 final, the FY2024 final of 60.0 IDR bn paid in 2025, and a similar sum for FY2025 paid in July 2026 [S4 p.102][S3]. Given the capex programme a low payout is the right allocation, and we would rather see cash retained than a dividend funded with debt. The board and the controlling family are substantially the same group of people, which is ordinary on IDX and is why we weight the related-party disclosure more than a governance score.

On ESG, the industry's central exposure is plastic. The company reports circular packaging content rising, has lifted the recycled content of its packaging and has launched lighter bottle formats and a fully recycled Eco Green line [S5][S4]. Water stewardship matters because the plants sit on springs and boreholes whose licences and recharge are a licence-to-operate issue, not just a cost. Both are disclosed, but neither is yet quantified in a way that changes the valuation; we treat them as medium-term licence risks rather than near-term costs.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the two fourth-quarter plant start-ups, the October 2026 SNI deadline, the FY2026 results in February 2027, the annual meeting and its dividend decision, and the first quarter of 2027 when the heat-driven base drops out [S5][S7][S4][S9].

Between updates we watch five numbers. Quarterly revenue growth against the category's mid-to-high single-digit band, because the whole thesis rests on CLEO growing faster than the category [S4 p.23]. Gross margin against the nine-month print, because that is the swing factor in the valuation [S2]. Capex including advances against the Rp645.0bn we forecast for FY2026E, because a programme that does not step down in FY2027 breaks the base case [S2]. The related-party share of trade payables, currently about a quarter [F8]. And the free-float position, because a resolution of the shortfall is the one event that could re-rate the shares without any change in the operating story [S0].

bear.narrative: The 2026 surge is the weather, not the franchise. The El Nino heat that GAPMMI credits for the double-digit category growth [S6] fades, the new capacity the whole industry is adding [S6] turns into a price war in single-serve, and CLEO's revenue growth falls to 8% in FY2027E and toward the category rate thereafter. Resin and packaging costs stay where the 9M2026 accounts put them and the mix keeps shifting to the lower-margin bottle, so gross margin stays at the 53.5% exit instead of recovering, and the company keeps spending on depots to defend share. The capex programme is not slowed, so free cash flow stays near zero and the dividend is held flat rather than grown. This is a value problem, not a funding problem: the balance sheet is not levered and operating cash flow covers the programme.

bull.narrative: The plant-and-depot programme is the growth engine, not a cost. The two Q4 2026 plants and the three 2026 openings [S5][S8] fill in Sumatra and Kalimantan where distribution is thinnest, so volume growth holds at 21% in FY2027E on a category growing 5-8% [S4]. Mandatory SNI certification from October 2026 [S7] raises the bar for the small producers that GAPMMI says are flooding the market [S6], and the certified national brands take the shelf space. Resin costs roll back, the bottle mix stabilises, and gross margin recovers toward the FY2024 peak; the capex peak passes a year early and free cash flow turns positive enough to lift the dividend.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +24.1% is arithmetic, not a forecast: 9M2026 net sales of Rp2,626.5bn [S2 p.7] plus a Q4 at +20% on Q4 2025's Rp732.4bn, which is a deliberate step down from the +28.7% Q3 printed against a heat-boosted base [S9][S6]. FY2027E +15.5% then fades to +9% by FY2030E: the company has outgrown the 5-8% AMDK category by roughly three times for three years [S4 p.23] and adds capacity every year (two plants in Q4 2026, three in 2026 [S5][S8]), but a 25% rate is a capacity-installation artefact, not a franchise rate, and the bottle segment's 29.7% [S9] is measured off a base that is about to get harder. The long-run rate is 4.5%, below the category's 5-8% because share gains cannot compound for ever.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: The cost links are zeroed, so these values are the margin the model prints. FY2026E 53.45% is 9M2026's actual 53.79% [S2 p.7] with a Q4 at Q4 2025's 52.36%; the 340bp fall from FY2025's 55.93% is real and structural - cost of goods sold rose 35.4% against a 25.5% revenue rise [S9] because the single-serve bottle segment (56.9% of sales) is growing faster than the refill gallon and carries more resin and packaging per litre [S9][F9][F10]. It recovers only to 54.6% by FY2030E as the three 2026 plants reach utilisation, and stays 370bp below the FY2024 peak of 58.3%: no margin expansion beyond a partial recovery is assumed.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed. The engine applies one deck move as a permanent scalar to every forecast year, and the only deck this name is tagged to is agricultural (cpo, soyoil, wheat, corn, soymeal). CLEO buys PET resin, preforms, closures and electricity; sugar enters only through the NOGU ready-to-drink tea line. Compounding a one-year agricultural deck view into a ten-year beverage margin would be an artefact. The resin exposure is carried explicitly in the gross margin path and discussed in section 2 [S2 p.7].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Not used: the share is zero. For completeness, AMDK is a price-competitive category where a listed producer competes with unbranded refill water and with Aqua and Le Minerale, so pass-through is partial and lagged - the 9M2026 record shows prices did not fully recover the resin and packaging inflation [S2][S9].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Zeroed for the same reason as link 1: no second deck series prices a material CLEO buys. Water is self-supplied from owned springs and boreholes and energy is domestic, so neither tracks an exchange-traded agricultural series [S4].

assumptions.label: Cost link 2: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Not used: the share is zero. Same partial and lagged pass-through logic as link 1 in a category where the refill gallon sets the reference price [S2][S9].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 34.51%: 9M2026 selling plus G&A was Rp891.5bn, or 33.94% of sales [S2 p.7], with Q4 at Q4 2025's 36.23% - the quarter that carries the heaviest advertising and the year-end distribution push. That is a real 2.8pp improvement on FY2025's 36.57%, the operating leverage the company points to when it says profit grew faster than sales [S5]. It eases to 33.3% by FY2030E as the depot and fleet base is spread over a larger revenue line, and no further leverage is assumed beyond that.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated, not taken from the pack: the FY2025 LK allocates Rp259.4bn of depreciation across COGS, selling and G&A [F1], and the nine-month 2026 charge is Rp207.2bn [F5], so FY2026E D&A is about Rp285.7bn on a Q4 run-rate, 8.15% of our revenue. That is more than the 5.2% the data pack implies from the direct-method cash flow. It drifts down to 7.19% by FY2030E as the three 2026 plants enter service and revenue outgrows the asset base.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is cash spent on fixed assets: acquisition of fixed assets Rp385.5bn plus advances on plant purchases Rp131.0bn, Rp516.5bn for 9M2026 [F6][F7]. The FY2026E Rp645.0bn is not a straight four-thirds annualisation of that total, which would be Rp688.7bn: the model annualises the fixed-asset line only (Rp385.5bn x 4/3 = Rp514.0bn) and adds the Rp131.0bn of advances as incurred, because advances are lumpy (Rp131.0bn in nine months against Rp55.3bn a year earlier) and we do not extrapolate a step-up in prepayments into Q4 [S2]. That is 18.4% of our FY2026E revenue. It is the peak of the build: three plants opened or opening in 2026 - Palu in Q3, Pontianak and Pekanbaru in Q4 [S8] - taking the network to 33 [S5]. It steps down to 12.2% by FY2030E and in perpetuity, against 11.6% in the previous draft. The terminal rate is set so the terminal year is internally consistent with its own growth and with the return we measure, not a better one: 4.5% growth at a 14% terminal ROIIC needs net reinvestment of 4.5/14 = 32.1% of NOPAT, or 5.2% of sales, and with D&A at 7.19% of sales and working capital absorbing 0.9% that is capex of about 12.2% of sales. A 17% terminal return, used before, was above the ~14% incremental after-tax return the FY2023-FY2025 record supports, so it understated terminal reinvestment; the reinvestment rate implied here is 32.1% of NOPAT and is stated in section 4. FY2025 was 14.8% of sales and FY2024 21.7% on the same cash-flow definition, exclusive of advances [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 30 September 2026 balance, not the FY2025 year end: operating working capital of Rp299.2bn on last-twelve-month revenue of Rp3,358.9bn is 8.9% [S2]. That balance flatters the ratio: other payables to third parties rose to Rp109.1bn from Rp5.4bn and taxes payable to Rp60.0bn from Rp12.7bn in the nine months [S2], and both reverse. We therefore let the ratio RISE toward 10.0% as those payables unwind and growth slows, rather than easing it down; a normalisation of payables is a cash outflow, not a release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 21.8%: the 9M2026 effective charge was Rp105.0bn on Rp482.1bn of pre-tax profit, 21.8% [S2 p.7], against the 22% statutory rate under UU HPP. FY2025 was 21.5% [S3].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 6.9%: 9M2026 finance costs of Rp22.2bn annualise to Rp29.6bn on opening debt of Rp426.8bn [S2 p.7]. The book is short-term working-capital loans, long-term bank debt and lease liabilities, so it reprices with the BI rate, which the macro desk holds at 5.75% [S2].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: 4.0%. Cash is small (Rp37.4bn at 30 September 2026) and the "others - net" line is a net expense, not income [S2], so the yield only matters for the interest-income line. 4% is the deposit rate on short rupiah balances.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero. Debt moved from Rp426.8bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp445.5bn at 30 September 2026, a Rp18.7bn drift, while nine-month operating cash flow of Rp565.8bn covered the Rp516.5bn capex programme and the Rp60bn dividend [S2 p.9]. We do not assume the balance sheet is levered up to fund growth.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: The "others - net" line is a recurring net expense of about Rp23bn a year (Rp23.3bn in FY2025, Rp23.9bn in FY2024, Rp17.1bn in 9M2026) - mostly FX on imported resin and packaging bought in dollars [S3][S2]. The nine-month 2026 run-rate annualises to Rp22.8bn, so we carry that rather than the Rp20bn of the previous draft.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 2.3%: minorities took Rp9.1bn of the Rp377.1bn 9M2026 profit, 2.42%, up from 1.97% in FY2025 as the group's plant subsidiaries with local partners earn more [S2][S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: 15.7%, the actual: Rp60.0bn of cash dividends paid in FY2025 on FY2025 profit attributable of Rp381.8bn [S3][S4 p.102]. The policy is not a ratio - the AGMS decides each year "in accordance with the Company's financial plans and capacity" [S4 p.102] - so the binding constraint is the capex programme, not a target payout. Holding the cash rather than distributing it is the right call while 18% of revenue goes into plants.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. 24,000,000,000 shares after the 1:1 bonus issue of May 2025, and no buyback, rights issue or new issuance announced [S3]. The 10.9% free float is below the exchange's 12.5% minimum, so the direction of risk is a controller sell-down, not dilution [S0].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.5% nominal, below the 5% house cap for rupiah models and below the 5-8% the company says the AMDK category grows [S4 p.23]: a mature bottled-water franchise should not outgrow Indonesian nominal GDP in perpetuity, and the terminal ROIC assumption already gives it credit for a durable brand and distribution position.

challenges.challenge: The reverse-DCF paragraph is wrong by two orders of magnitude. The report says Rp370 requires 'revenue growth of about 0.2% every year'; the engine's reverse_dcf returns implied FY2027E revenue growth of 0.1651 (16.5%) against the 0.155 (15.5%) base. The 0.165 was read as 0.165%, and the solve covers FY2027E only, not every year. As written a reader is told the market prices near-zero growth when it prices growth one point above our base.
challenges.answer: Reverse-DCF paragraph rewritten: the solve is stated as FY2027E revenue growth of 17.8% against our 15.5% base, on one period and one variable, with {{rev.implied_value}} and the increment {{rev.factor}} shown; the 0.165-as-0.165% error and the 'every year' claim are gone [S2].

challenges.challenge: The P/E cross-check (Rp395, 30% of the blend) applies 21.32x, the average of the 9.63x median of all 26 FOOD_BEVERAGE tickers in the model's peer set and a 33.0x own-history mean built on four annual observations; EV/EBITDA applies 13.0x = average(7.06x peer median, 18.94x own history). Neither component is disclosed, and 21.3x is called 'how Indonesian investors actually price consumer names' when it is 2.2x the peer median and above the stock's current 18.9x. At the covered-peer median (ADES/CMRY/ICBP/INDF/MYOR = 8.9x) the P/E value is about Rp178 and the 60/30/10 blend about Rp280: the ADD does not exist without the own-history premium.
challenges.answer: Both multiple components and their n are now disclosed in section 4, the own-history 33x is rejected as an anchor (four observations, pre-de-rating), and the weights move from 60/30/10 to 70/20/10 with the reason stated; the covered-peer read is disclosed as the low end of the cross-check range [S0].

challenges.challenge: The model never states the reinvestment rate or ROIIC for the forecast years (method-card output contract), and its terminal capex of 11.2% of sales is derived from a 17% terminal ROIIC while §3 tells the reader incremental after-tax returns are 'in the low to mid teens' with no numbers and no source. The card requires excess returns to fade toward WACC by year 10; here terminal returns are assumed above the measured level, which lifts terminal value. At a 14% ROIIC terminal reinvestment would be 32% of NOPAT rather than 26.5%: about Rp65bn a year of terminal FCFF, roughly Rp15/share, 4% of the DCF.
challenges.answer: Terminal ROIIC cut from 17% to the top of the measured low-to-mid-teens range; terminal capex_pct 11.2% to 12.2% so the terminal year is consistent with 4.5/14 = 32% reinvestment of NOPAT; the forecast reinvestment rate (capex less D&A plus NWC over NOPAT) is now stated in section 3 and section 4 [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The 0.5pp COE premium is described in fund record as 'the smallest addition that brings COE and WACC to the bottom of the mandated band': it is calibrated to the band, not derived from priced risk. Without it COE is 10.70% and WACC 10.45%, and the model's own grid (WACC -0.5pp, g 4.5%) gives a DCF of Rp374.5, above the Rp370 price. The report's central framing, 'our DCF says Rp343, below the market', therefore depends on the fitted add-on. The rationale also rests on figures that cannot all be true: insider 92.87% + free float 10.9% + institutions 0.30% = 104.1%.
challenges.answer: The premium is now sourced to the documented house IDR COE/WACC band rather than 'the smallest addition', and the body states plainly that the un-premiumed DCF (the WACC -0.5pp grid row) sits just above the price; the ownership arithmetic (92.87 + 10.9 + 0.30) is withdrawn and replaced with the Tancorp majority and the float alone [S0][S4 p.70][S10].

challenges.challenge: The model's registry profile (registry_asof 2026-10-27) records the exchange minimum at 15% with an interim 12.5% step due 31 March 2027 and the final 15% by 31 March 2028, HSC listing and exclusion from the IHSG calculation announced 20 October 2026, MSCI's freeze on Indonesian index increases and its Emerging-to-Standalone consultation. The report treats the float as 'a structural fact ... not a temporary one', calls the rule 12.5%, and gives no deadline and no mechanism. A controller sell-down or placement to meet a 4.7-month deadline is a dated supply event and a bear input.
challenges.answer: Section 5 and 6 now state the 12.5% step by 31 March 2027 and 15% by 31 March 2028 with the rule source, and treat the controller sell-down as a dated supply event; the IHSG exclusion and MSCI removal are stated as the registry profile records them and flagged as not sourceable in an archived filing, so the re-rating is a conditional bull leg, not a base driver [S10][S0].

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality section is built on FY2025 and misses the 30 September 2026 balance. 9M2026 operating cash flow of Rp565.8bn against net profit of Rp377.1bn was helped by 'other payables - third parties' rising from Rp5.4bn to Rp109.1bn (+Rp103.7bn), taxes payable from Rp12.7bn to Rp60.0bn and accrued expenses +Rp7.4bn, all of which reverse. Trade receivables rose from Rp120.5bn to Rp188.3bn (+56.3% against revenue +25.5%, 2.2x, tripping the card's 1.5x flag) and inventory from Rp305.4bn to Rp442.1bn (+44.8% against COGS +35.4%); the report says 'Inventory has tracked cost of goods sold closely' and never connects the build to the auditor's inventory existence/valuation KAM [S3 p.5]. The three-year accruals claim cites only the FY2025 LK, which has one comparative year.
challenges.answer: Earnings-quality section rebuilt on the 30 September 2026 balance: the payables and tax timing that flattered operating cash flow is named and quantified in the text, the receivables and inventory divergence against revenue and COGS is disclosed, the auditor's inventory KAM is connected to the build, the FY2023 cash flow is cited to the filing that carries it, NWC now RISES to 10% as payables unwind, and the bear carries an inventory write-down haircut [S2][S3 p.5].

challenges.challenge: §3 says 'The data pack carries FY2025 depreciation of 259 IDR bn and FY2024 of 208 IDR bn, which is what the direct-method cash flow shows and is barely half the real charge.' The pack carries Rp146.93bn and Rp119.65bn (model restated block; fund record says 'the data pack printed Rp146.93bn'); 259.44/208.38 are the restated LK values. The sentence is self-contradictory and misstates the pack by 76%, so a reader cannot reproduce the restatement that the whole margin and multiple work depends on.
challenges.answer: Depreciation sentence rewritten: the pack printed Rp146.9bn for FY2025 and Rp119.7bn for FY2024 and the note allocates Rp259.4bn and Rp208.4bn; the 259/208 figures are no longer attributed to the pack, so the restatement is reproducible [F1][F2][S3 p.59].

challenges.challenge: The 25/55/20 weights are asserted, with bear above bull despite 9M2026 revenue +25.5%, profit +20.6% and the bottle segment +29.7%, and no evidence for 25 vs 20. Doubling the bear weight (bear 50, base 30, bull 20) gives a target of Rp386 and a 5.1% expected return, below the ADD threshold, so the rating rests on an untested weight. §5 also quotes the bear and bull at Rp255 and Rp564 (today's values) while the target uses Rp281 and Rp624, without labelling which is which.
challenges.answer: Weights are now 22/56/22 - no skew against a bull the 9M evidence supports - scenario values are labelled today's value versus twelve-month target, and the weight test is disclosed: bear at 50% weight gives an expected return below the ADD threshold, and with the DCF primary the rating is HOLD on either weight [S2][S9].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex of 18.4% of sales is the 9M2026 cash figure (Rp385.5bn fixed assets + Rp131.0bn advances = Rp516.5bn) simply annualised; advances are lumpy (Rp131.0bn in nine months against Rp55.3bn a year earlier) and there is no evidence Q4 repeats the 9M run-rate, so peak capex may be overstated by Rp50-100bn, understating FY2026E FCFF of Rp162bn and the 'cash-consuming build' narrative. The same advances-inclusive definition is not applied to history: FY2025's 14.8% is the cash-flow 'acquisition of fixed assets' line only. The BLOCK justification also counts 'three plants ... and two more start in Q4 2026' (five), while §1 says three (Palu Q3; Pontianak and Pekanbaru Q4) and S8 says the three bring the total to 32.
challenges.answer: QC justification corrected to three plants (Palu Q3, Pontianak and Pekanbaru Q4, total 32 then 33), the double count removed, and the definitional mismatch disclosed: FY2024/25 on the cash-flow fixed-asset line, FY2026E advances-inclusive, which overstates the peak [S5][S8][F6][F7].

challenges.challenge: The October 2026 SNI deadline is treated only as a cost/execution risk. The report never quantifies the upside that a fixed compliance cost spread over 33 plants gives against the single-plant producers GAPMMI says are flooding the market [S6][S7]. It also treats the sub-minimum float only as a risk, not as the dated catalyst in its own registry: a controller sell-down to reach 12.5% by March 2027 raises the float, and a float above the index threshold is the one route to a re-rating for a name excluded from the IHSG.
challenges.answer: The float remedy is added as a dated bull leg with its condition (12.5% by 31 March 2027, 15% by 2028) and the SNI effect is labelled narrative only - a fixed compliance cost that favours the 33-plant network but is not quantified in the model [S7][S10].

challenges.challenge: Both the base fade and the bull's 21% are asserted: there is no per-capita consumption, penetration, market-share or litres/plant-utilisation build, so a reader cannot tell whether FY2027E growth of 15.5% (down 8.6pp from FY2026E with three plants opening and 500 nodes) is capacity-constrained or a default haircut. The compounder card requires growth to be tied to reinvestment and ROIIC and says per-capita S-curves justify duration; neither is done. An unsourced haircut below the last actual and below the company's own 20% plan is what the base-case card forbids.
challenges.answer: The fade is sourced to the plant programme: three 2026 additions taking the network to 33 and 500 distribution nodes, with the FY2027E rate below the 20% plan because the 2026 base includes the heat effect; reinvestment rate and ROIIC are now stated, though we still do not build litres or utilisation by plant - the pack does not disclose them [S4 p.23][S5][S8].

challenges.challenge: Three inputs point the wrong way. The assumptions call the 340bp gross-margin fall 'real and structural' yet the model recovers 1.15pp to 54.6% by FY2030E with no source for the recovery; 'others - net' is carried at -Rp20bn against -Rp23.3bn in FY2025 and a -Rp22.8bn 9M2026 run-rate, understating the recurring expense; and payout is set at 15.5% when Rp60.0bn on Rp381.8bn of FY2025 profit is 15.7%.
challenges.answer: Payout set to 15.7% (Rp60.0bn on Rp381.8bn), other non-operating items to the -22.8bn 9M2026 run-rate, and NWC reversed to rise as payables normalise; the 1.15pp margin recovery is retained but sourced to the three 2026 plants reaching utilisation, with no expansion beyond that partial recovery [S3][S2].

challenges.challenge: The investment summary still says the 9M2026 cash capex of Rp516.5bn (F6 Rp385.5bn fixed assets + F7 Rp131.0bn advances) was 'roughly a fifth of annualised revenue'. 9M2026 revenue is Rp2,626.5bn, so annualised revenue is ~Rp3,502bn and the ratio is 14.7%; 19.7% is the ratio to nine-month revenue. QC FIX Q10 was left unanswered and the sentence is unchanged in fund record.
challenges.answer: Investment summary now reads that the 9M2026 cash capex of F6 plus F7 was roughly a fifth of nine-month revenue (about fifteen per cent of annualised revenue). The 14.7% is against annualised revenue of Rp3,502bn; the fifth is the ratio to the Rp2,626.5bn nine-month base, which a reader can reproduce from the same statement [S2]. The modelled 18.4% of FY2026E revenue in section 3 is untouched.

challenges.challenge: The assumptions inputs.capex_pct basis says the 9M2026 advances-inclusive Rp516.5bn 'annualises to about Rp646bn'. That is 516.5 x 1.25; a 9M annualisation is x4/3 = Rp688.7bn. The modelled Rp645.0bn actually equals the fixed-asset line annualised (Rp385.5bn x 4/3 = Rp514.0bn) plus the Rp131.0bn of advances, which is the defensible treatment given lumpy advances, but the sentence as written cannot be reproduced and no Q4 estimate explains the 1.25x.
challenges.answer: inputs.capex_pct basis rewritten to state what the model does: the fixed-asset line annualises to Rp514.0bn (Rp385.5bn x 4/3) and the Rp131.0bn of advances is added as incurred, giving Rp645.0bn or 18.4% of FY2026E revenue, because advances are lumpy (Rp131.0bn in nine months against Rp55.3bn a year earlier) and are not extrapolated into Q4 [S2]. flags.justification: The move down from FY2026E to the terminal year is the build cycle, not a modelled improvement. Capex is 18.4% of sales in FY2026E because three plants are opened or opening in 2026 - Palu in Q3, Pontianak and Pekanbaru in Q4 - taking the total to 33 [S5][S8]; nine-month 2026 cash capex was already Rp516.5bn of fixed assets plus advances [F6][F7]. There are three plants, not five: the earlier justification double-counted the Q4 pair, and section 1 was right. The programme is finite - a fixed number of plants a year on a growing revenue base - so the ratio falls as the denominator grows and the build finishes. FY2024 and FY2025 are on the cash-flow fixed-asset line only, FY2026E on the advances-inclusive definition; the step-down therefore overstates the FY2026E peak by the advances, which we accept as the conservative side. The terminal rate is the rate that makes the terminal year consistent with its own 4.5% growth at the measured terminal return on new capital, not a held-forward peak [S3][S2].
